facts.value: Biomedical sciences are a set of sciences applying portions of natural science or formal science, or both, to develop knowledge, interventions, or technology that are of use in healthcare or public health.

The primary focus is the biology of human health and disease, ranging from the generic study of biomedical sciences and human biology to more specialised subject areas such as pharmacology, human physiology and human nutrition.

It is underpinned by relevant basic sciences including anatomy and physiology, cell biology, biochemistry, microbiology, genetics and molecular biology, pharmacology, immunology, mathematics and statistics, and bioinformatics.

The healthcare science workforce is an important part of the UK's National Health Service (NHS). While people working in healthcare science are only 5% of the staff of the NHS, 80% of all diagnoses can be attributed to their work.
The four governments of the UK have recognised the importance of healthcare science to the NHS, introducing the Modernising Scientific Careers initiative.

Biomedical Science is a branch of science that understands the biological principles that govern the functioning of the human body and helps in finding new and distinct ways to cure the disease by developing advanced diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies.
